tagline: Rock, woods and rolling country along the St. Croix valley
intro: The St. Croix Scenic Byway stretches 124 miles between a point north of Sandstone and Point Douglas, near Hastings. Explore Minnesota presents the drive as a journey through the St. Croix Wild and Scenic River Valley, with rock, cliffs and woods in the north giving way to rolling ground and long views in the south.

An earlier route through this country was the Point Douglas to Superior Military Road, begun by the federal government in the 1850s for troop movement. Civilian and commercial traffic followed, but Minnesota inherited the unfinished road at statehood in 1858 without the money to complete it. A surviving 1.2-mile section became part of the trail system at Wild River State Park. Rough and unfinished as it was, the military road remained the best route north until railroads arrived in 1870. At Interstate Park, later highway construction took a different form: U.S. Route 8 descends through a rock cut blasted in 1931.

Traveling south, begin with Sandstone on the Kettle River and Hinckley on the Grindstone River. At Taylors Falls, Interstate Park straddles the basalt gorge of the St. Croix. Continue through Stillwater on the river’s west bank to Point Douglas, where the St. Croix meets the Mississippi.

moments.title: Hinckley
moments.text: Hinckley’s fire museum occupies a replacement: the railroad depot was rebuilt just after the 1894 fire on the same spot, as an exact replica of its predecessor. The first railroad reached Hinckley in 1869, beginning an expansion of logging and rail traffic. On September 1, 1894, a firestorm destroyed Hinckley and other northeastern Minnesota towns, killing more than 400 people in and near the town. Agriculture then became central to recovery, with potatoes, fruits and vegetables among the crops. The museum tells the story of the fire and the recovery.

moments.title: Interstate State Park
moments.text: Glacial potholes puncture the basalt at the Dalles of the St. Croix, where two state parks face each other across the river. Sand and gravel swirling in powerful eddies drilled into the rock; larger stones polished the shafts. The narrow gorge and sharp turn at Angle Rock later caused repeated logjams during the lumber era. Road builders also worked through the basalt: U.S. Route 8 descends through a cut blasted in 1931, followed by stone overlooks and guardrails in the mid-1930s. The logjams themselves became visitor attractions, drawing as many as a thousand tourists a day.
moments.notice: Glacial potholes mark the basalt beside the St. Croix gorge.

moments.title: Stillwater
moments.text: Stillwater takes its name from the calm river near the town center, a name proposed in 1843 by first-sawmill builder John McKusick. Rafts of logs came down the St. Croix, gathered at the boom site upstream and passed through the town’s sawmills. In 1848, a territorial convention at Myrtle and Main streets began the process toward Minnesota statehood. Minnesota became a separate territory the following year and a state in 1858. The lift bridge across the St. Croix was completed in 1931, with Minnesota and Wisconsin sharing its construction cost equally.
